Implement `keep` and `discard`, which split a collection by a predicate, without the standard library's filter.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/strain) (MIT). Listed under [Collections & Algorithms](/examples/?subject=collections-and-algorithms).

```nomi-run
// FILE: strain.nomi
//# The exercise asks for `keep` and `discard` without the standard
//# library's filter, so `keep` walks the list with a pattern.

/// The items of `list` that `predicate` holds for, in order.
pub fn keep<T>(list: List<T>, predicate: (T) -> Bool) -> List<T> {
    case list {
        [] -> []
        [head, ..tail] when predicate(head) -> [head, ..keep(tail, predicate)]
        [_head, ..tail] -> keep(tail, predicate)
    }
}

/// The items of `list` that `predicate` does not hold for, in order.
pub fn discard<T>(list: List<T>, predicate: (T) -> Bool) -> List<T> {
    keep(list, &(not predicate(&1)))
}

// FILE: strain_test.nomi
import strain

test "keep integers" {
    cases: List<#(String, List<Int>, (Int) -> Bool, List<Int>)> = [
        #("keep on empty list returns empty list", [], fn _x -> True, []),
        #("keeps everything", [1, 3, 5], fn _x -> True, [1, 3, 5]),
        #("keeps nothing", [1, 3, 5], fn _x -> False, []),
        #("keeps first and last", [1, 2, 3], &(&1 % 2 == 1), [1, 3]),
        #("keeps neither first nor last", [1, 2, 3], &(&1 % 2 == 0), [2]),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, list, predicate, expected), description {
        assert strain.keep(list, predicate) == expected
    }
}

test "keeps strings" {
    words = ["apple", "zebra", "banana", "zombies", "cherimoya", "zealot"]

    assert strain.keep(words, &String.starts_with(&1, "z")) == ["zebra", "zombies", "zealot"]
}

test "keeps lists" {
    lists = [[1, 2, 3], [5, 5, 5], [5, 1, 2], [2, 1, 2], [1, 5, 2], [2, 2, 1], [1, 2, 5]]

    assert strain.keep(lists, &List.contains(&1, 5)) == [
        [5, 5, 5],
        [5, 1, 2],
        [1, 5, 2],
        [1, 2, 5],
    ]
}

test "discard integers" {
    cases: List<#(String, List<Int>, (Int) -> Bool, List<Int>)> = [
        #("discard on empty list returns empty list", [], fn _x -> True, []),
        #("discards everything", [1, 3, 5], fn _x -> True, []),
        #("discards nothing", [1, 3, 5], fn _x -> False, [1, 3, 5]),
        #("discards first and last", [1, 2, 3], &(&1 % 2 == 1), [2]),
        #("discards neither first nor last", [1, 2, 3], &(&1 % 2 == 0), [1, 3]),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, list, predicate, expected), description {
        assert strain.discard(list, predicate) == expected
    }
}

test "discards strings" {
    words = ["apple", "zebra", "banana", "zombies", "cherimoya", "zealot"]

    assert strain.discard(words, &String.starts_with(&1, "z")) == ["apple", "banana", "cherimoya"]
}

test "discards lists" {
    lists = [[1, 2, 3], [5, 5, 5], [5, 1, 2], [2, 1, 2], [1, 5, 2], [2, 2, 1], [1, 2, 5]]

    assert strain.discard(lists, &List.contains(&1, 5)) == [[1, 2, 3], [2, 1, 2], [2, 2, 1]]
}
```

## How it's written

- `keep` is a `case` over `[]` and `[head, ..tail]`, with a `when` guard on the arm that keeps the head. Each kept item is consed onto what the rest keeps, so the order is the input's with no reverse.
- `discard` is `keep` with the predicate negated, `&(not predicate(&1))`, so the walk is written once.
- Both are generic over the item type, which the canonical data asks for with integers, strings and lists of integers. The integer cases are two `subtests` tables, one per function, whose predicate column is a function value, `(Int) -> Bool`; the string and list cases are one test each, since a table's columns have one type.
- The canonical predicates are written as captures (`&(&1 % 2 == 1)`, `&String.starts_with(&1, "z")`, `&List.contains(&1, 5)`), and the constant ones as `fn _x -> True`.
